📍 How to find your coordinates manually Open Google Maps on your phone, long-press your location, and read the coordinates shown at the top of the screen. Then enter them above.
Open Google Maps →
  1. Long-press your current location on the map
  2. Coordinates appear at the top — e.g. 46.1936, 6.2386
  3. First number = Latitude (positive = N, negative = S)
  4. Second number = Longitude (positive = E, negative = W)
  5. Enter the absolute values above and select N/S and E/W

Sky Conditions
—
—
▾
—
ADU (Analog-to-Digital Units) is the raw brightness number your sensor records for each pixel. A lower sky background ADU means less light pollution — your target has less noise to compete against. The percentage shows how bright the sky is relative to your sensor's maximum capacity.
—
Target Exposure
—
—
▾
—
Headroom is how much space remains before your sensor is full. Too little (under 10%) means bright areas will clip and lose detail — reduce your sub length. Sky-limited means the sky background noise dominates, which is ideal — stacking more subs is the most efficient way to improve your image.
—
Integration Progress
—
—
▾
—
SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio) measures how clearly your target stands out from the background noise. SNR 20 gives a good quality image. SNR 30 is excellent. Each additional sub you stack improves SNR — but with diminishing returns. Going from 1 to 4 subs doubles SNR; going from 4 to 16 doubles it again.

📖 Feature Guide
JD'S DEEP SKY CATALOG · HELP
No results found
GETTING STARTED
Smart Pick mode
The default view. Scans all 12,160 OpenNGC objects and ranks them for your active location and rig tonight. Objects are scored on visibility, altitude and framing — best targets rise to the top.
Full Catalog mode
All 12,160 objects from the OpenNGC database, sorted by magnitude. Use type, month, rig and search filters to narrow down. Curated objects are marked ❆.
Setting your location
Tap the location button in the header. Add a site with coordinates and Bortle class, or tap GPS to auto-fill. Switch between sites instantly — all calculations update live.
Setting your rig
Select a rig from the filter bar to activate scoring. Framing scores, Smart Pick ranking and the best rig column all respond to your active rig selection.
THE CATALOG
79 curated objects
Hand-scored objects with per-rig ratings (0–5), filter recommendations, and observational notes written for Cork 51.9°N. Notes adapt dynamically when you switch location.
❆ badge in Full Catalog
Objects marked ❆ are in the curated catalog. Clicking them opens the full detail pane with rig scores, filter notes and the session logger.
Rig scores 0–5
5 = ideal framing for that FOV. 4 = good. 3 = workable. 2 = marginal. 1 = possible but not recommended. Scores reflect framing quality, not object difficulty.
Framing score ⚙
In Full Catalog mode, framing scores are auto-computed from rig FOV ÷ object angular size. Clearly labelled as estimated — select a rig to activate.
Latitude warning
If your active site is more than 10° from Cork, a banner notes that scores and notes were written for 51.9°N and may not apply at your latitude. Dynamic calculations (altitude, visibility) are always accurate.
MONTHLY VISIBILITY
Visibility strip
12 dots or bars, one per month. Green = good (object above 35° altitude). Amber = marginal (20–35°). Grey = poor or below horizon from your active location.
Month filter
Click any month to filter to objects visible that month. Works in both Smart Pick and Full Catalog modes. ALL shows everything above the horizon.
Circumpolar toggle
Filters to objects that never set from your location. From Cork (51.9°N) this means dec ≥ 58.1° — these targets are available every night of the year.
TONIGHT PANEL
Night-definition dropdown
The Tonight panel lets you choose what "night" means via a per-site dropdown (Astronomical / Nautical / Civil / Entire), inspired by Telescopius. Astronomical (sun below -18°, default) is the conservative astrophotography choice. Nautical (-12°), Civil (-6°) and Entire (sun below horizon) progressively relax the threshold — useful at high latitudes in summer when astro-dark doesn't happen. Each site remembers its own choice.
Filter-aware imaging recommendations
When no astro-dark window exists, the imaging recommender adapts to your filter. Broadband + star-color + quadband filters get the recommendation withheld (sky-brightness model has no twilight term). Duoband filters show with a borderline caveat. Tight narrowband (L-Ultimate, L-Synergy, Antlia Tri-Band II) shows clean. Click "Why?" on any banner for the physics.
FILTERS
L-QEF
Broadband LP filter. Passes the full visual spectrum with mild LP reduction. Best for galaxies, globular clusters and open clusters where colour accuracy matters.
L-Ultimate (2nm)
Dual narrowband — passes Hα and OIII only. Transforms emission nebulae from light-polluted sites. Not suitable for galaxies or star clusters.
L-Synergy
Quad narrowband — Hα, OIII, SII and Hβ. Excellent for complex emission regions. Stronger LP rejection than L-Ultimate.
Triband
Passes Hα, OIII and Hβ. Good all-round narrowband for emission targets. Less restrictive than L-Ultimate.
L-Para
Broadband with enhanced LP blocking. Good balance between broadband versatility and LP rejection.
Duo-Band (Dwarf)
Hα + OIII dual narrowband for the Dwarf units. Essential for emission nebulae from light-polluted sites.
SKY MAP
Opening the Sky Map
Header button 🌌 Sky Map opens the all-sky planisphere overlay. Stereographic-zenith projection centred on the active site at the chosen time. Horizon = unit circle, N / E / S / W at the rim (N highlighted in gold as the north reference).
Dot colour = object type
Dots are coloured by catalogue type to match the main page type pills: GAL = violet, NEB = aqua (dark / reflection / emission all share this), PN = sky blue, SNR = orange, OC = yellow, GC = coral. Same palette wherever you see object types in the app.
Top-50 tonight highlight (moon-aware)
The 50 atlas targets with the best predicted sky background at the slider time render as larger, more opaque dots. Ranking metric is moon-aware (Krisciunas & Schaefer 1991): targets near a bright moon are demoted, anti-moon targets are promoted, and on moonless nights ranking falls back to peak altitude tonight. Type colour is preserved — rank is encoded by size + opacity. Smaller, dimmer dots are the rest of the atlas above the horizon.
Moon dot + phase shading
When the moon is above the horizon at the slider time, it's drawn as a cream disc with a shadow part that matches the current phase — terminator orientation follows the sun direction, so a waxing gibbous on the map looks like a waxing gibbous through the window. Always shown when astronomically up, even if your horizon profile blocks its azimuth (the moon still brightens the rest of the sky via atmospheric scatter). Hover for illumination % and altitude.
Mosaic Planner (ASIAIR export)
Open it from the header (▱ Mosaic) or the “Plan mosaic” button in an object’s detail pane. Pick one of your ASIAIR rigs (FMA180 / Askar V60 & V80 / 91F with your ASI cameras — smartscopes plan mosaics in their own apps), set columns × rows × overlap and an optional rotation. It builds the ASIAIR mosaic plan (Center + each pane with RA / Dec / Angle) to Copy or Download as a .txt for ASIAIR’s Plan → Mosaic import. “Rotate panes to preserve alignment” (on by default) gives per-pane angles for a clean great-circle grid; off keeps one fixed camera angle. The to-scale preview draws the target’s real shape (outline or measured ellipse) under the pane grid and flags when a target fits in one frame. Exposure per pane defaults to the Imaging Settings sub-length recommendation and is editable. Geometry validated against a real ASIAIR export.
The Mosaic Inspector
Open it from the header (🔭 Inspector, next to Mosaic). Drop in your captured lights (.fit / .fits) — as many as you like; subs of the same panel are grouped automatically, and a selected-files list shows what you picked. It reads each frame’s plate-solve (WCS) to draw the real on-sky footprints — so you can confirm in the field, before teardown, that every pane landed and left no coverage gap. If you saved a plan in the Mosaic Planner, it overlays the planned panes (dashed) under the actual footprints and red-shades any planned pane not yet covered. A second pass bins, sky-subtracts and reprojects the frames into a rough grey composite (asinh / midtone / linear stretch) you can Save as PNG. Everything runs on-device — nothing is uploaded; on mobile the FITS you download from the ASIAIR all land in one folder, so select them together. A framing quick-look, not a stacker. Use ✕ Clear on the file list to start over; when a saved mosaic plan is present, the bar under the footprint says whether it is overlaid or hidden and lets you forget it (offering to save it first). The composite labels each panel with its frame name, and a coverage line flags any interior gaps with a one-click supplementary plan to fill them.
Where's my selected target on the Sky Map?
Pick any object from the catalogue and open the Sky Map — it marks that target with a teal crosshair reticle and name label at its position in tonight’s sky, so you can see where it sits. This works for any of the 15,810 catalogue objects, not just the five Smart Pick plans (which keep their coloured rings). The crosshair tracks the time slider and is hidden only when the target is below your horizon.
FOV comparator (multi-rig overlay)
An Equipment-Key strip sits below the time slider — click "+ Add rig ▾" to pick rigs (grouped by scope) and overlay their FOV rectangles on the selected target. Each rig gets a stable colour and stroke pattern (solid / dashed / dotted) so the same rig is always recognisable across sessions; the Key card shows the colour swatch + rig name + dimensions, and the polygon on the chart matches by stroke colour and pattern. Click × on a key card to remove a rig. No cap on rigs — overlay as many as you want; the user controls visual clutter. Real angular size, no exaggeration (zoom 1×–10× to inspect narrow rigs). Camera rotation locked at 0° (sensor long axis east-west). RA offsets cos(dec)-compensated; corners falling below your horizon project past the horizon circle. Active rigs persist in localStorage across sessions.
Why are FOV rectangles tilted?
The rectangles align with the celestial coordinate grid (sensor short axis = N-S, long axis = E-W — the "north-up" convention every processing pipeline produces). On a zenith-projection sky chart, celestial north points in different directions across the sky, so the rectangle's tilt at any target is the parallactic angle for that target's current position. Move the time slider to watch it rotate as the sky rotates. The framing is accurate to the final processed image whether you're on an equatorial mount or letting a smartscope's pipeline derotate the stack — this IS the patch of sky your image will cover.
What's the dashed amber ring near the zenith?
It marks the alt-az tracking limit at altitude ~75°. Above this line, alt-azimuth-mounted scopes (the default mode for Dwarf 3, Dwarf Mini, Seestar S50/S30/S30P, Celestron Origin Home) suffer field rotation that degrades tracking and stacking — raw frames show star trailing and stacked output loses corner detail. If your mount is in EQ mode (most modern smartscopes support EQ via firmware + an appropriate EQ tripod head), ignore the ring — EQ mounts have no field rotation by design. Brands without EQ support today: Vaonis Vespera, Unistellar.
Time slider
Sweeps from dusk → astro-dark → dawn over the active site's night window (twilight ladder: astronomical → nautical → civil → sun-below-horizon falls back automatically at high latitudes in summer). The displayed time renders in the site's own timezone.
Zoom + pan
Mouse wheel zooms 1× → 10× around the cursor (capped per DEF-077 to stay below a Chromium compositor cliff at very high zoom). Click-drag (or touch-drag) pans. Double-click anywhere on the sky resets, or use the ⊙ Reset button next to the time readout. Constellation lines stay sharp at any zoom (non-scaling stroke).
Click a dot → jump to detail
Clicking any DSO dot closes the Sky Map, opens its detail pane, and narrows the main catalog list to that one row (search box gets the object id). Clear the search to restore your prior list context.
Horizon obstruction respected
If you've configured a horizon profile (trees, buildings, etc. — see Horizon Editor), the Sky Map respects it: dots, stars, constellation lines and labels in blocked sectors are culled. The blocked region itself is shaded dim grey (or dim red for fully-disabled sectors) so an empty patch reads as "your horizon blocks this" rather than "the map is broken".
Constellation labels
Each IAU constellation has its name rendered at the centroid of its stick-figure (89 entries — Serpens stored as Caput + Cauda). Labels show only when the centroid is above 8° altitude and clear of any obstruction sector. Stars at mag ≤ 1.6 carry their proper names (Sirius, Vega, Arcturus, ...).
HORIZON EDITOR
Why a horizon profile
Trees, buildings, mountains — most observing sites have something blocking part of the sky. The Horizon Editor lets you describe each location's horizon as 8 azimuth sectors (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) with a minimum altitude per sector and an enabled/disabled toggle. Smart Pick and the Sky Map honour this when ranking and rendering tonight's targets.
Opening the editor
Open the Locations panel from the header → click the ✎ edit icon on any site → Horizon. The editor opens as an overlay with a compass-rose visualisation and a per-sector list.
Per-sector altitude + enabled toggle
Click any sector (on the rose or in the list) to edit it. The slider sets the minimum altitude clear sky starts at (e.g., 25° if there's a treeline). The "Include this direction" toggle disables the sector entirely (e.g., a house wall blocking the entire azimuth wedge from horizon to zenith).
Quick presets
Open (no obstruction — same as default), Suburban (mild ~15° everywhere), Valley (high east + west, low north + south), South only (everything except S blocked — useful for north-facing balconies). Apply then refine per sector.
Live stats — Visible Sky % + Targets Tonight
The footer of the editor shows how much of the celestial hemisphere is reachable from your profile, and how many of the curated targets would survive the obstruction filter tonight. Helps gut-check whether a setting is too aggressive.
How the profile is used
Smart Pick uses it to filter out targets whose nighttime trajectory never enters a clear sector at observable altitude. The Sky Map uses it to cull dots, stars, constellation lines and labels behind your horizon, and to shade the blocked sky regions. Toggling ⛰ Horizon: on/off in the header bypasses the filter temporarily without losing the profile.
SKY ANALYSIS
Upload FITS / XISF files
Drop .fit, .fits, or .xisf files into the Light Frame or Dark Frame zone. The tool parses headers for exposure, gain, filter, object and date. .xisf masters (mono or RGB, UInt16 or Float32) work as well as raw FITS subs — useful for measuring SNR on integrated masters. Compressed XISF blocks aren't supported — re-export uncompressed if needed.
What is "MRS dB"?
MRS = Multi-Resolution Support — the wavelet-noise estimation method (Starck & Murtagh 1994) used here and in leading astro processing software. MRS dB is 10·log10(signal²/noise²) measured on a B3-spline wavelet decomposition of your sub. Higher is better; the metric is dominated by sky background at light-polluted sites, so MRS dB alone overstates quality under Bortle 6+.
Sky conditions
Computed from the measured sky background vs your Bortle class expectation. Good / Marginal / Poor — updates with each sub added.
Target exposure
Estimates whether your subs are long enough to be sky-noise limited. Short subs waste read noise budget relative to sky noise.
SNR progress
Tracks cumulative SNR across your session. Shows how many more subs are needed to reach a useful detection threshold.
Session log offer
After FITS files load, a pre-filled log form appears automatically. Object, date, filter, integration and gain are read from headers. Tap confirm or skip — non-blocking.
Dwarf filename parser
Parses DwarfLab filenames (e.g. SH2-157(1)_60s100_Duo-Band_20260213-202050_13C.fits) to extract temperature and mosaic panel index — not in the FITS header.
SESSION LOGGER
Logging a session
Click any curated object, scroll to Sessions, tap Add Session. Or accept the auto-offer after uploading FITS files in Sky Analysis.
Export backup
Data panel → Export. Saves all sessions, locations and rig overrides as a JSON file. Data lives in your browser only — back up regularly.
Import
Data panel → Import. Merges sessions and locations with existing data. Shows a dry-run preview before applying.
Backup reminder
The tool reminds you to export after every 10 new sessions, and when closing the Data panel if no backup in 30+ days. Two-step inline confirmation prevents accidental dismissal.
DATA PANEL
Catalog integrity
Shows 79 curated + ~15,810 atlas objects (12,159 OpenNGC + 313 Sharpless + 3,338 DEF-071 ingest: LDN + LBN + VdB + Barnard + WR), plus a SHA-256 fingerprint of the curated catalog (id, mag, ra, dec). Green ✓ OK means data is unmodified.
